title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
This page belongs to the 'Additamentum' of the 1783 paper, as printed in Opuscula Analytica I. The aim of the Additamentum is to give firmer proofs of the quadratic-residue observations made earlier. Write D for the prime divisor.

(1) Proof of Theorem 2. Let D = 4p - (2q+1)^2 be prime. Then (2q+1)^2 + D = 4p, so 4p ≡ (2q+1)^2 (mod D). Hence 4p is a quadratic residue. Since 4 is a square, p is a residue, by the rule that if α^2β is a residue then β is one.
Because D ≡ 3 (mod 4), -1 is a non-residue. Euler puts this as: for divisors 4n-1 no residue occurs with both signs. Therefore -p is a non-residue.

(2) §6. Since p is a residue, some x^2 - p y^2 is divisible by D. So D must have the shape that divisors of x^2 - p y^2 must have.

(3) §7. Since -p is a non-residue, no x^2 + p y^2 with D not dividing x, y is divisible by D. So D is excluded from the linear forms that contain the divisors of x^2 + p y^2. This links residue symbols to the theory of divisors of quadratic forms.

(4) §8. This is Euler's criterion. With D = 2m+1, p^m ≡ 1 (mod D). It rests on §4: the m residues form a set closed under multiplication, and the powers of p lie in it. Since D = 4n-1, m = 2n-1 is odd. So (-p)^m = -p^m ≡ -1, and D divides p^m + 1, not (-p)^m - 1. This agrees with -p being a non-residue.

(5) Theorem 3 (§9). If P = 4n+1 is prime, every number n - q^2 - q and every number q^2 + q - n is a quadratic residue mod P.
Proof: write P = 4p + (2q+1)^2, which gives p = n - q - q^2. Then Theorem 1 (§1) shows that both p and -p are residues. In modern terms, 4(q^2+q-n) = (2q+1)^2 - P ≡ (2q+1)^2, and -1 is a residue mod P.

(6) §10-11. As q runs over 0, 1, 2, ..., these values reduce to at most 2n distinct residues. Euler asserts that they give all the residues. This is true: q^2 + q - n ≡ ((2q+1)/2)^2 (mod P), and (2q+1)/2 runs through every class mod P. He then begins noting closure under products and powers, which is continued on the next page.

Purpose: these are the lemmas behind the Scholion on the next page. There Euler conjectures, and checks numerically, that every prime factor of q^2 + q - n is a residue mod 4n+1. That conjecture is the content of quadratic reciprocity for primes P ≡ 1 (mod 4).
errors: Theorem 2 tacitly assumes D does not divide p. With D = 4p - (2q+1)^2 this can fail, for example D = 3, p = 3, q = 1, or D = 7, p = 14, q = 3. Then p ≡ -p ≡ 0, and the claim that -p is a non-residue fails trivially. Theorem 1 has no such problem, since there D > 4p.

§8 relies on the §4 argument for p^m ≡ 1 (mod 2m+1). That argument has a gap. Knowing that the powers of p lie among the m residues only bounds the order of p by m. It does not show the order divides m. A Lagrange-type coset argument or a Fermat-based argument is needed; Euler had supplied such arguments in earlier papers, but not here.
§10 says there are 2n residues. That counts nonzero residues; the forms can also produce 0, when P divides 2q+1. This is harmless.

ideas.what: For a prime D = 4p - (2q+1)^2, p is a quadratic residue and -p a non-residue; for D = 4p + (2q+1)^2, both ±p are residues
ideas.modern_name: elementary quadratic-residue lemma via the representation D = 4p ∓ square; first supplement (-1 | D)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1783 Opuscula Analytica; the -1 supplement goes back to Euler and Fermat)
ideas.where_published: Opuscula Analytica I (1783), Additamentum; related material in E552

ideas.what: A residue or non-residue p corresponds to the existence or absence of divisors of x^2 ∓ p y^2
ideas.modern_name: link between Legendre symbols and representation by quadratic forms or divisors of binary forms
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (theory of divisors of quadratic forms), later Lagrange and Legendre
ideas.where_published: E164, E256 and related papers on divisors of x^2 + N y^2

ideas.what: p^m ≡ 1 (mod 2m+1) for a residue p; sign analysis when m is odd
For a prime 4n+1, the values ±(q^2 + q - n) run through all quadratic residues
ideas.modern_name: q^2 + q - n ≡ ((2q+1)/2)^2 (mod 4n+1); a parametrization of the squares
ideas.where_published: Opuscula Analytica I (1783); discussed in histories of quadratic reciprocity (e.g. Lemmermeyer, Weil)

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains standard lemmas from Euler's well-known late treatment of quadratic residues. That treatment leads to his formulation of reciprocity in terms of the prime factors of q^2 + q - n, which historians already discuss. Nothing here appears absent from the literature.
